content: A hypertensive crisis refers to a sudden and severe elevation in blood pressure, which may or may not be accompanied by acute end-organ damage. This condition is broadly categorized into hypertensive urgency and hypertensive emergency. The most common cause of a hypertensive crisis is noncompliance with prescribed antihypertensive medications. Classification Hypertensive crises are classified based on the presence or absence of acute end-organ damage: Hypertensive Urgency: This is characterized by a severe elevation in blood pressure without evidence of acute end-organ damage. Hypertensive Emergency: This involves a severe elevation in blood pressure (systolic ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic ≥ 120 mmHg) accompanied by acute end-organ dysfunction. Examples of such dysfunction include hypertensive encephalopathy, eclampsia, aortic dissection, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary edema, acute myocardial infarction, acute renal failure, or symptomatic microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Causes Hypertensive crises are life-threatening and require immediate treatment regardless of the underlying cause. Common causes include: Withdrawal from antihypertensive medications (e.g., beta-blockers, clonidine). Noncompliance with antihypertensive therapy. Pheochromocytoma. Adverse effects of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Use of stimulants such as cocaine, methamphetamine, or phencyclidine (PCP). Hypertensive crises can occur de novo or as a complication of essential or secondary hypertension. Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) A focused initial rapid evaluation (FIRE) is essential to identify patients requiring immediate intervention. Red flags indicate the need for urgent management. Complete Diagnostic Approach After the initial rapid evaluation and initiation of urgent interventions, a comprehensive diagnostic approach should be undertaken to determine the underlying cause and guide further management. Treatment Management of hypertensive crises is guided by the recommendations of the Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee (JNC 7). Initial Approach Intravenous Antihypertensive Drugs: Use short-acting, titratable IV antihypertensive agents for precise control of blood pressure. Oral Antihypertensive Drugs: Oral agents may be considered in less severe cases. Examples include: PO furosemide 20 mg (repeat as necessary). PO nifedipine SR 30 mg (single dose). PO felodipine 5 mg (single dose). Management of Specific Hypertensive Emergencies Hypertensive emergencies are best managed with continuous infusion of short-acting, titratable antihypertensive agents. Avoid sublingual and intramuscular routes of drug administration due to their unpredictable pharmacodynamics. Assess the patient’s volume status before initiating IV vasodilators to prevent excessive drops in blood pressure. Key Recommendations Dos Use continuous infusion of short-acting, titratable antihypertensive agents for hypertensive emergencies. Carefully monitor the patient’s response to therapy and adjust treatment accordingly. Don’ts Do not use nifedipine, nitroglycerin, or hydralazine as first-line therapies due to their potential toxicities and adverse effects. Avoid intramuscular or sublingual antihypertensive medications in hypertensive emergencies. Do not administer rapid-acting antihypertensive agents outside of an ICU setting.
